report:
Based on my research, your conclusion is correct: current high-quality evidence does not support CoQ10 as an effective treatment for Parkinson's disease movement symptoms.

**Summary of evidence:**

Early, smaller studies raised hope. A 2002 phase II trial (Shults et al.) suggested high-dose CoQ10 (1200 mg/day) might slow functional decline in early Parkinson's disease compared to placebo, and a small 2003 study by Müller et al. reported "mild symptomatic benefit." These promising but preliminary results prompted a larger, definitive trial.

That larger trial—the NIH-funded QE3 study (Beal et al., published in *JAMA Neurology*, 2014)—was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 600 mg/day and 2400 mg/day CoQ10 in early Parkinson's disease patients. It was stopped early for futility: neither dose showed any benefit over placebo on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), the standard measure of motor and functional symptoms. The study concluded there was "no evidence of benefit" and that CoQ10 should not be pursued further for this indication (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261061585_A_Randomized_Clinical_Trial_of_High-Dosage_Coenzime_Q10_in_Early_Parkinson_Disease_No_Evidence_of_Benefit).

A subsequent meta-analysis (Liu et al., *Neurological Sciences*, 2016) pooling multiple randomized controlled trials found that, in aggregate, CoQ10 did not produce statistically significant improvement in UPDRS scores relative to placebo, reinforcing the negative findings from the definitive trial (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9).

A more recent systematic review (2022, *Journal of Personalized Medicine*) confirms that while CoQ10 levels are altered in PD patients and CoQ10 has theoretical antioxidant/mitochondrial rationale, clinical trial evidence for symptomatic or disease-modifying benefit remains lacking (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975).

**Conclusion:** Despite biological plausibility (mitochondrial support, antioxidant effects) and early encouraging pilot data, the best available evidence—a large, rigorous, NIH-sponsored RCT and subsequent meta-analyses—shows CoQ10 does not improve Parkinson's disease movement symptoms.
